# STAC time stacks and stacgrid {#sec-stac}

`odc.stac.load()` does more than read. It snaps a grid, groups items by solar day, chooses
overviews, merges overlaps, and returns an xarray cube. To find out exactly what it does, GA's
tutorial load (45 IW bursts, HH, solar day, 200 m EPSG:3031) was done three ways, and every
difference was traced to a choice.

## Three loaders, two choices

| Loader | Overviews when downsampling | Overlaps | Equal to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `odc.stac.load()` 0.5.3 | read (`-ovr AUTO`) | first valid pixel wins | per-item `gdal.Warp`, defaults, first-wins: 0 pixels differ (GDAL 3.8.4 and 3.12.2) |
| GDAL STACIT mosaic, warped | not available through the VRT | last valid wins | per-item `gdal.Warp`, `overviewLevel="NONE"`, last-wins: 0 of 226,943 differ |

Nearest-neighbour from 20 m to 200 m: the overview choice changes nearly every value, by up to
10 dB; the merge order changes only the burst overlaps, about 9% of pixels. STACIT has no time
axis, so each solar day is its own search. It was no shorter than plain `osgeo.gdal` (78 lines
against 92) and slower (about 29 s against 12 s; odc 6 s).

## stacgrid

[`stacgrid/`](https://github.com/mdsumner/geo-stack-alt/tree/main/stacgrid) is the layer
`osgeo.gdal` lacks for STAC time stacks. It's about 300 lines in Python (`osgeo.gdal`, numpy,
the standard library) and the same in R (`gdalraster`, `jsonlite`, `curl` for POST), with the
same functions:

| Step | Function |
|---|---|
| Search a STAC API (GET; POST when `intersects=` is given; follows `next`) | `stac_search()` |
| Items from a STAC-GeoParquet file (OGR; needs `libgdal-arrow-parquet`) | `items_from_geoparquet()` |
| Grid: bbox in the target CRS, snapped out to the resolution | `grid_from_bbox()` |
| Grid: copy an existing raster's (odc's `geobox=`) | `grid_from_raster()` |
| A grid's outline in lon/lat, to search with | `grid_footprint()` |
| Group: `"solar_day"`, `"time"`, a property, or a function | `group_items()` |
| Warp each group's items onto the grid and merge, in parallel | `stac_load()` |
| An asset's `raster:bands` scale and offset | `scale_offset()` |
| A band name to (asset, band): `"red"`, `"visual.2"` | `asset_band()` |

GA's tutorial load in Python (from
[`ga_py.py`](https://github.com/mdsumner/geo-stack-alt/blob/main/cleanroom/experiments/stacgrid/ga_py.py)):

```python
import stacgrid as sg
BBOX = (73.5, -69.1, 74.0, -68.8)
items = sg.stac_search("https://explorer.dev.dea.ga.gov.au/stac", ["ga_s1_nrb_iw_hh_1"],
                       bbox=BBOX, datetime="2021-01-01/2021-03-01")
grid = sg.grid_from_bbox(BBOX, "EPSG:3031", 200)
groups = sg.group_items(items, "solar_day", grid=grid)
out = sg.stac_load(groups, ["hh_gamma0", "oa_layover_shadow_mask"], grid, workers=8)
# out["hh_gamma0"]: a (group, y, x) numpy array
```

The R functions have the same names and arguments. Every choice that changes pixels is an argument, with odc-stac's
behaviour as the default:

- `overviews="AUTO"` reads a coarser overview when downsampling (gdalwarp's and odc-stac's
  default); `"NONE"` always reads full resolution, as STACIT does.
- `fuse="first"`: in overlaps the first valid pixel in (datetime, id) order wins, as odc-stac;
  `"last"`: the last wins, as a VRT mosaic.
- `scale=True` applies **each item's own** scale and offset before the merge.
- `group_items(items, "solar_day", grid=grid)` uses odc-stac's solar-day rule; without `grid`,
  each item's own longitude.

On Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 its defaults equal `odc.stac.load()` in every pixel, from both
languages, and Python equals R in STACIT mode too.

## Parallel reads

`stac_load(..., workers=8)` runs the per-item warps in threads (Python; GDAL releases the GIL) or
forked processes (R, `parallel::mclapply`). The merge still goes in item order, so pixels can't
depend on which warp finishes first. GA tutorial load, 45 items, GDAL 3.8.4, wall time including
the search, two passes:

| workers | 1 | 4 | 8 | 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 11.3, 12.0 s | 3.9, 3.9 s | 2.9, 2.8 s | 2.6, 2.6 s |
| R | 12.6, 12.9 s | 8.3, 8.1 s | 5.3, 5.8 s | 4.4, 4.0 s |

`odc.stac.load()` on the same load: 6.4 s. Every run, both languages, every worker count: 0
pixels differ from odc-stac.

## GA's fast-ice notebook loads

GA's fast-ice notebooks (`abradley60/fast-ice` 4694c6c) load EW scenes from a
STAC-GeoParquet index and IW scenes from DEA's STAC API. stacgrid against the notebooks'
odc-stac calls (pixi, GDAL 3.13.3):

| Notebook load | Items | Grid | Groups | Python, R vs odc-stac |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sentinel_1_load_demo`: IW from the API, ±6 days, `intersects=` a sample's footprint | 15 | from the sample GeoTIFF, 1702 × 1627 at 40 m | `sat:relative_orbit`: 2 | 0 of 2.9 M differ |
| same, EW from STAC-GeoParquet, ±1 hour | 1 | same | 1 | 0 of 2.8 M |
| `fast_ice_from_stac_xarray`: EW from STAC-GeoParquet, 2019 | 60 | bbox at 77.6°S, 1683 × 1407 at 40 m | `time`: 60 | 0 of 141.9 M |
| same, IW from the API, `intersects=` the bbox outline | 150 | same | solar day: 30 | 0 of 69.0 M |

Same item IDs, same grid, every case. Wall time for the xarray notebook's loads: odc-stac 68 s,
stacgrid Python 77 s, R 114 s (R includes writing the stacks to GeoTIFF).

Getting there exposed three things:

- **POST.** The API wants `intersects` as JSON in a POST body; DEA's explorer accepts POST
  without advertising it, and GET with `intersects` is a 400.
- **GDAL's Parquet bbox pre-filter** drops items silently ([chapter @sec-versions]).
- **odc-stac's solar-day rule** uses one longitude for the whole load, the grid centre, and
  whole hours, `int(lon / 15)`. Passes near local midnight split differently from a per-item
  longitude: 150 IW items at 167°E give 30 groups this way and 60 with per-item fractional hours.

## Scale and offset

odc-stac 0.5 ignores `raster:bands` scale and offset and returns stored values. Applying one
offset afterwards is wrong wherever a group mixes items with different offsets.

Earth Search `sentinel-2-l2a`, red band near Hobart, December 2021 to February 2022, 10 m: 23
items in 17 solar-day groups. Scale is 0.0001 throughout; offset is 0 for processing baseline
03.01 and -0.1 from 04.00. Late-2021 dates have two items, the original and a reprocessing, so
**6 of the 17 groups mix offsets.**

| | vs stacgrid `scale=True` (Python and R) |
|---|---|
| Reference: odc loads each item alone, scaled with its own metadata, merged first-valid in odc's order | 0 of 3.9 M pixels differ |
| odc `groupby="solar_day"` raw, then offset -0.1 for all | 2.29 M differ, by 0.1 |
| odc raw, then offset 0 for all | 1.60 M differ, by 0.1 |

Merge order within a group is (datetime, id), as odc-stac sorts. Two duplicate pairs have
identical datetimes, so the id decides; ordering by search order instead changed 449,890 pixels.

## Multi-band assets

Bands are named as odc-stac names them: `"visual.2"` is band 2 of asset `visual`. The bands asked
for from one asset come from one warp per item.

Earth Search's `visual` asset (TCI: 3 bands, uint8, nodata 0 in the file) describes its bands
in `eo:bands` only. odc-stac 0.5.3 counts bands from `raster:bands` or STAC 1.1 `bands`, so it
sees one band: `"visual"` loads band 1 as float32 with no nodata, and `"visual.2"` raises
`KeyError`. stacgrid reads the band count from the file. With `raster:bands` added to the items
so that odc could serve as the reference, all five requested bands
(`visual.1`-`.3`, `visual`, `red`) were equal: 0 of 27.3 M pixels, Python and R.

## What it doesn't replace

odc-stac and xarray give lazy, chunked (dask) loads and the xarray ecosystem. stacgrid loads
eagerly into numpy and is meant for the area and time ranges notebooks like GA's use. For
continent-scale lazy cubes, odc-stac remains the tool. The point is pinning and explicit
choices, not avoiding it.
